unobservable: The second parameter (the separator). main() only ever invokes the 1-argument form, so the default "-" is the only separator ever exercised. Nothing can be learned about a custom separator ('_', '.', a multi-character string, or the empty string): whether it is appended as a whole string or as a single char, whether an empty separator is legal, and whether an alphanumeric separator would then itself be re-processed are all UNOBSERVABLE.

Whether leading and/or trailing separators are stripped from the result. The template hard-codes the prefix "The " and suffix " Test", so the result invariably begins with 't' (from 'The') and ends with 't' (from 'Test'). No choice of W can put a separator at either end of the string handed to parameterize, so a strip/trim step (as Rails' parameterize performs) is indistinguishable from its absence. I tried every avenue I could construct — leading spaces, all-space W, all-punctuation W, W consisting only of hyphens, and the `--` argv trick — and none can produce a boundary separator. UNOBSERVABLE.

Whether the implementation squeezes separators ONLY at the string boundaries. Interior runs are provably not squeezed (10 spaces -> 10 hyphens), but boundary runs cannot be created, so a boundary-only squeeze is UNOBSERVABLE (it is subsumed by the strip question above).

Behavior on embedded NUL (0x00). execve terminates each argv element at the first NUL, so W=$'a\x00b' reaches the program as "a" (observed output 'the-a-test'). Whether parameterize would delete an interior NUL, treat it as a terminator, or emit a separator is UNOBSERVABLE through a command-line argument.

Whether the character classification uses <cctype> isalnum/tolower with the global locale versus hardcoded ASCII range comparisons. Behavior is identical under LC_ALL=C, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, tr_TR.UTF-8 and en_US.ISO-8859-1, which rules out any locale sensitivity in practice, but the two implementations are behaviorally identical here so the internal mechanism is UNOBSERVABLE (and irrelevant).

Whether signed-char UB exists in an isalnum()/tolower() call for bytes >= 0x80. Every high byte is deleted under every locale tested, so no such misbehavior is exposed; the presence or absence of the latent bug is UNOBSERVABLE.

Any behavior for |W| beyond ~1.5 x 10^5 bytes: the kernel's ARG_MAX rejected the exec at |W| = 600000 ("Argument list too long") before the program ran, so the upper limit / allocation behavior for multi-megabyte inputs is UNOBSERVABLE.

Whether parameterize is implemented in terms of downcase/dasherize/other Inflector helpers, or standalone. Only the composite input->output mapping is observable; internal call structure is UNOBSERVABLE (and disassembly was out of scope).

result.pseudocode:
########################################################################
# 1) underscore(s)  -- CONFIRMED EXACTLY. Pure, stateless, per-byte map.
#    No lookahead, no lookbehind, no acronym grouping, no locale,
#    no UTF-8 awareness, no separator rewriting, no length limit.
########################################################################

function underscore(s):            # s is a byte string (may be empty)
    out = ""                       # byte buffer
    for i = 0 to length(s) - 1:
        c = s[i]                   # single byte, 0x01..0xFF (0x00 unreachable via argv)
        if c >= 0x41 and c <= 0x5A:        # ASCII 'A'..'Z' -- the ONLY special class
            if i > 0:
                out = out + "_"            # 0x5F, unconditionally (see notes)
            out = out + (c + 0x20)         # ASCII-lowercase the byte
        else:
            out = out + c                  # EVERY other byte: copied verbatim, unchanged
    return out

# Equivalent, output-identical formulations (indistinguishable -- see `unobservable`):
#   (a) "if i > 0"                          <- stated above
#   (b) "if out is non-empty"               <- identical, because no byte is ever dropped
#   (c) "always emit '_' before an uppercase byte, then strip one leading '_' at the end"
# Formulations that are REFUTED (do NOT use):

# =====================================================================
# Everything below is BYTE-oriented. There is no character/codepoint
# awareness anywhere: no UTF-8 decoding, no locale case mapping.
# Verified against the binary on 1100 randomized inputs + ~400 targeted
# probes: 0 mismatches.
# =====================================================================

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- split
FUNCTION split_on_underscore(s):
    # '_' (0x5F) is the ONE AND ONLY separator byte.
    # Confirmed by an exhaustive scan of bytes 0x01..0x7F placed between
    # two letters: ONLY 0x5F split. NOT '-', '.', '/', ' ', ':', '::',
    # TAB(0x09), LF(0x0A), '\', and NOT any byte 0x80..0xFF.
    # Empty fields ARE produced; runs of '_' are NOT collapsed at split.
    RETURN s.split('_')          # n underscores -> n+1 fields

# ------------------------------------------------- per-segment upcasing
FUNCTION upcase_first_byte(seg):
    IF seg == "": RETURN ""
    b := seg[0]                  # a single BYTE, not a codepoint
    IF b >= 0x61 ('a') AND b <= 0x7A ('z'):
        seg[0] := b - 0x20
    # EVERY other byte value is emitted UNCHANGED: 0x01..0x60
    # (controls, TAB, LF, space, digits, all punctuation, 'A'-'Z', '@',
    # '[', '\', ']', '^', '_', '`'), 0x7B..0x7F, and ALL of 0x80..0xFF
    # (UTF-8 lead AND continuation bytes). Verified for all 128..255.
    RETURN seg
    # seg[1..] is NEVER modified -> the tail of a segment is NOT
    # lowercased. "aBCdef" -> "ABCdef", "bAr" -> "BAr", "FOO" -> "FOO".

# ------------------------------------------------------------- camelize
FUNCTION camelize(s, upper_first):
    # line 3 exercises the upper_first == FALSE path.
    parts := split_on_underscore(s)
    out := ""
    FOR i FROM 0 TO len(parts)-1:
        seg := parts[i]
        IF seg == "":
            CONTINUE                       # empty segment contributes NOTHING
        IF i == 0 AND upper_first == FALSE:
            out := out + seg               # field 0 passed through un-upcased
            # UNOBSERVABLE whether this branch also lowercases seg[0] or
            # all of seg: field 0 of line 3's input is literally "test",
            # already all-lowercase. What IS observed: it is NOT upcased
            # (output byte 0 is 't' = 0x74, never 'T').
        ELSE:
            out := out + upcase_first_byte(seg)
    RETURN out
    # NO acronym table (id->Id, html->Html, http->Http, url->Url,
    #   api->Api, xml->Xml, json->Json, css->Css, ip->Ip, tcp->Tcp,
    #   sql->Sql, uuid->Uuid, db->Db, io->Io, ui->Ui, ssl->Ssl,
    #   cli->Cli, gui->Gui  -- all plain first-byte upcasing).
    # NO '/' -> '::' translation.  NO whitespace trimming.
    # NO length limit observed (tested to ~900 bytes, 600 segments).

# ------------------------------------------------------------- classify
FUNCTION classify(s):
    t := singularize(s)      # classic Rails order; a VERIFIED NO-OP for
                             # every input reachable through this template
                             # (see note below) -> presence UNOBSERVABLE
    RETURN camelize(t, upper_first = TRUE)

# For all inputs observable through line 5, classify reduces exactly to:
#     concat( upcase_first_byte(f) for f in s.split('_') if f != "" )
# i.e. it is camelize with upper_first = TRUE; every non-empty segment,
# INCLUDING the first, gets its first byte upcased.
#
# classify does NOT strip namespaces:
#   leading "::" is KEPT and, because ':' is not in [a-z], the following
#   letter is NOT upcased: "::foo_table" -> "::fooTable".
#   Text before '.' or "::" is KEPT: "lib.models.Foo_table" ->
#   "Lib.models.FooTable"; "Admin::User_table" -> "Admin::UserTable".
#
# SINGULARIZE NOTE: line 5's input always ends in the literal "_table",
# so the final segment always renders "Table". Across 600 random inputs
# every line-5 output ended in "Table" (0 exceptions), and no earlier
# segment was ever singularized ("cats_table" -> "CatsTable", NOT
# "CatTable"; "cities_table" -> "CitiesTable"; "people_table" ->
# "PeopleTable"). The library's singularize IS non-trivial (line 2 shows
# "cities"->"city", "boxes"->"box", "statuses"->"status"), but it only
# fires on a trailing 's', which "..._table" never has. So a singularize
# step is either absent or a no-op; the two are indistinguishable here.
